Welcome to the November 2026 Power BI feature summary! We're sharing this month's updates ahead of the Power BI Desktop release, which will follow the week of November 23, 2026.
This month’s updates make it easier to build, customize, manage, and share experiences across Power BI and Microsoft Fabric. Highlights include expanded ways to work with Microsoft Copilot, new reporting and visualization capabilities, enhancements to org apps, and updates that simplify data connectivity and semantic model deployment.
Read on to explore the latest features and see how they can help you create more consistent, interactive, and accessible experiences with your data.

Learn more about the DataViz World Championships.
General 
Retiring standalone Power BI Copilot experiences in favor of Microsoft Copilot (Preview)
The next chapter for Microsoft Copilot in Power BI and Fabric. We're expanding Microsoft Copilot in Power BI and Fabric to users without a Copilot Premium license. This is the next step toward replacing standalone Power BI Copilot with Microsoft Copilot.
Figure: The Microsoft Chat experience in Power BI; available capabilities depend on your license and entitlements.
The path from standalone Power BI Copilot. We plan to end support for standalone Power BI Copilot on the web, including Home, and in Teams and Power BI mobile by the end of January 2027. These experiences remain available during the transition. Official deprecation, end-of-support, and retirement dates have not been announced; we will share dates and guidance separately. Microsoft Copilot is the planned replacement, with capabilities based on each user's license and entitlements. Report Copilot remains available and supported in the Power BI service, Power BI Desktop, and Power BI mobile. Copilot in web modeling and DAX query view also remains available and supported.
An upgraded experience built around your Fabric data. Power BI and Fabric users without an M365 Copilot Premium license will be able to use Fabric IQ in Microsoft Copilot in the Power BI service even with just a Basic license, subject to their content permissions and licensed access.
Refer to the licensing and eligibility requirements for the applicable access conditions.
With Fabric IQ in the Basic experiences, users can:

Find and reference supported reports by name, link, or attachment.
Ask questions grounded in Power BI semantic models and explore results through follow-up questions.
Return to conversation history across supported Copilot experiences.

Basic licenses include Fabric IQ, but not Work IQ. Premium adds Work IQ for organizational Microsoft 365 emails, meetings, chats, and documents, plus features such as advanced model access.
For more information on the breakdown, refer to the Copilot in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric (Preview) documentation.
Updated Copilot defaults on December 8, 2026. Microsoft Copilot is currently off by default; administrators can enable it in the Fabric admin portal. Admins can manage access with the "Users can access Microsoft Copilot in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric" tenant setting in the Fabric admin portal.
On December 8, 2026, Microsoft Copilot will default to on and standalone Power BI Copilot will default to off. Existing administrator choices will be preserved. This changes tenant-setting defaults only; it is not a deprecation, end-of-support, or retirement date.
Figure: Visual of the Microsoft Copilot tenant setting in the Fabric Admin portal.
Get started
Explore the current preview and administrator requirements in Copilot in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric. For more about how Copilot answers questions using Power BI data, refer to Fabric IQ in Copilot Chat.
Retiring app-scoped Copilot (Preview) in Power BI workspace apps
We're retiring app-scoped Copilot (Preview) in Power BI workspace apps. The experience and the workspace app setup setting used to enable it will be removed in January 2027.
Figure: App-scoped Copilot entry point in a Power BI workspace app navigation menu.
Your app content, audiences, and permissions will remain unchanged. You can continue using Copilot within eligible reports, including reports opened in a workspace app, to ask questions about your data and get summaries.
Power BI Desktop for Apps (Preview)
We're building a new way to turn your Power BI data into interactive Fabric apps.
Power BI Desktop for Apps combines your semantic model with an AI-assisted app-authoring experience. Start with your data, describe the experience you want to create, and work with the built-in agent to build and iterate on your app. You can then preview your app locally and continue refining it yourself.

As you build, a live connection to your semantic model in the Power BI service gives the agent context about your data. You can also edit text directly and use the Design pane to adjust fonts, colors, themes, and other visual properties.
Power BI Desktop for Apps is being prepared for preview and is coming soon. Learn more.
Reporting
Improved performance for the Power BI add-in in PowerPoint
Presentations with multiple Power BI add-ins can now use less memory and load faster. We've improved the Power BI add-in for PowerPoint to reduce its memory footprint and load times, helping PowerPoint handle more Power BI content in a presentation. If you've tried the add-in before, try it again with a presentation that includes several Power BI reports or visuals.
Power BI Integration with OneDrive and SharePoint (Generally Available)
First introduced in 2023, in preview, the Power BI integration with OneDrive and SharePoint has reached general availability.
Many report authors already use OneDrive and SharePoint to store and collaborate on their Power BI files before publishing them. With this release, both the web viewing experience and the open, save, and share capabilities in Power BI Desktop are ready for production use, so your reports can live where the rest of your Microsoft 365 work already does. 
View Power BI files right in OneDrive and SharePoint 
Quickly view Power BI files stored in OneDrive and SharePoint directly in your browser, with no need to install Power BI Desktop or download the file. Just select a .pbix file in your OneDrive or SharePoint library and the report opens in the browser, where you can interact with visuals, explore the data, use bookmarks, switch page views, and apply high-contrast colors. 

Share with confidence: share a link using the familiar Microsoft 365 share dialog, which respects your OneDrive and SharePoint permissions and policies. 
Built-in version history: track changes and restore earlier versions of a report with Microsoft 365 version history. 
Governed by default: sensitivity labels are respected, and admins have visibility through Microsoft 365 audit logs and the Power BI activity log. 

Figure: Power BI reports can be viewed directly in SharePoint or OneDrive.
Open, save, and share from Power BI Desktop 
Power BI Desktop works seamlessly with OneDrive and SharePoint. Open reports straight from your OneDrive or SharePoint sites, save new or existing reports directly to a cloud location, and share a link with colleagues using the Share button at the top right of Power BI Desktop. Storing your files in OneDrive and SharePoint gives you file versioning, easier co-authoring, and a backup that's always in the cloud. 
Figure: Open Power BI files from OneDrive, SharePoint, or your recent files in Power BI Desktop.
 Getting started 

Viewing in the browser is on by default. Admins can manage it under Tenant settings > Integration settings in the admin portal: “Users can view Power BI files saved in OneDrive and SharePoint”.
Open, save, and share in Power BI Desktop are on by default in the November release of Power BI Desktop. Admins can manage it under Tenant settings > Integration settings in the admin portal: “Users can share links to Power BI files stored in OneDrive and SharePoint through Power BI Desktop”.
To view reports in the browser, you need a Power BI Pro, Premium Per User, or E5 license and at least read access to the file. 

Try the Power BI integration with OneDrive and SharePoint and learn more about it in our documentation: View Power BI files in OneDrive and SharePoint and Power BI Desktop OneDrive and SharePoint integration.
Card visual trend charts
Show trends or regional patterns alongside your key metrics in the Card visual. Use a line, bar, or column chart to show changes over time, or a shape map to show regional patterns. To get started, add a field to Trend axis (Preview) in the Build pane. Add measures to compare performance and a legend to identify them. Customize data labels, markers, axes, and other formatting options; tooltips show the data point and axis values.
Figure: The Card visual supports line, column, bar, and shape map charts, with chart and formatting options visible in the Format pane.
Learn more about Card visual trend charts in the Create a card visual in Power BI documentation.
Add to style presets (Generally Available)
Visual style presets let you format a visual once and reuse that formatting for every visual of the same type in your report. Instead of repeating the same changes on each chart, format one visual in the Format visual pane, and then save it as a named style preset or add it to the base visual style.
Figure: Save a visual’s current formatting as a named style preset to reuse across visuals of the same type.
The preset then appears in the Style presets dropdown for every visual of that type, so you can apply the same look with a single selection. You can also make any preset the default for its visual type, and visuals that use the default style update to match. Style presets are saved in your report's theme. To reuse them in other reports, download the theme and import it there.
After saving a style preset, use Reset all style settings to default to remove manual formatting overrides and let the visual use its preset. This new option appears alongside Reset all settings to default and removes only formatting set in the Format visual pane. It preserves conditional formatting, actions, and data-bound elements, such as reference labels.
Figure: Reset formatting overrides to use the visual’s style preset without removing conditional formatting, actions, or data bindings.
Learn more about creating, updating, and sharing presets in the Use visual style presets in Power BI reports documentation.
List slicer with multi-line selection box and dropdown (Generally Available)
The list slicer helps you save space on your report page with a customizable dropdown. Format items with pictures, labels, and conditional formatting, and keep that formatting in dropdown mode. Adjust the dropdown size to fit your report. Selections appear as pills that readers can review and remove. To show more selections before they're grouped into a count pill, turn off Single line under Selection box > Layout.
Figure: WithSingle lineturned off, the selection box fills the visual and shows more selections before they're grouped into a count pill.
Use show selected first to list selected items at the top, making them easier to find in long lists. This option works in the list slicer with or without dropdown mode and is also available in the button slicer.
Learn more about creating and using a list slicer.
Gantt chart updates (Preview)
Make overall progress and individual task progress easier to see in the Gantt visual with column totals and data labels. Configure totals under Columns > Totals and data labels under Rows > Data labels in the Format visual pane. This release also fixes progress bar formatting and keyboard navigation issues and increases default column widths to give task details more room.
Figure: Show overall progress with column totals and display progress percentages beside task bars using data labels in the Gantt visual.
 Learn more about using the Gantt visual in Power BI.
Table and matrix filtering from action buttons within visual title (Preview)
Bring filtering to where report viewers are working with the new Filter action button for table and matrix visuals. Adjust visual-level filters directly on the visual, with the same experience and filter card formatting as the Filters pane. The Filter action button also shows the number of visual-level filters applied to the visual.
To enable it, turn on Action buttons under General in the Format visual pane. Position the button within the title, above, or below, and customize its icons, text, and styling to fit your report. The overlay shows only Filters on this visual; page and report filters are still adjusted in the Filters pane.
Figure: Add a Filter action button so readers can adjust visual-level filters directly from a table or matrix without opening the Filters pane.
For now, this is limited to table and matrix visuals, and we plan to bring it to other visuals in a future release. Action buttons are planned to expand with a Sort button in a future release too.
Learn more about adding action buttons to Power BI visuals.
Slicer mode (date picker, dropdown, list) can be set using custom theme (Generally Available)
Set the slicer mode in a custom report theme to apply a consistent default without configuring each slicer individually. Save the setting in your theme file, then reuse the theme in other reports to keep your preferred slicer experience consistent. If the specified mode isn't compatible with the slicer's column, Power BI automatically switches to a compatible mode.
Learn more about setting visual properties in custom report themes.
Default slicer mode for dates is now “date picker” (Generally Available)
When you add a date column to the Slicer visual, it now starts in Date picker mode, so you can offer flexible date filtering without changing the style first. Readers can choose a specific date or range using the calendar or slider, or use relative selections anchored to today, the first date, or the last date in your data. You can still choose another style under Slicer settings > Options > Style in the Format pane.
Learn more about using the Date picker slicer.
Icons visibility improvements for high contrast mode (Generally Available)
Conditional formatting icons now adjust to display correctly in high contrast mode, making it easier to distinguish status indicators and interpret your data when using high contrast settings.
Figure: Conditional formatting icons now adapt to high contrast mode, including in the icon picker.
Learn more about using high contrast colors in Power BI reports.
Blank reports in the web communicate better next steps (Generally Available)
When you edit a blank report on the web, you now see the same getting-started experience as in Power BI Desktop.
Figure: The blank report canvas on the web now shows the same getting-started guidance as Power BI Desktop, helping authors build visuals from their data.
If a report is intentionally blank with no visuals, viewers see a banner explaining that it's empty, so they don't mistake the blank canvas for content that's still loading.
Figure: A banner lets report viewers know when a report is empty and suggests adding visuals or contacting the report owner.
Learn more about viewing and editing reports in the Power BI service.
Azure Maps support for sovereign clouds (Generally Available)
Azure Maps in Power BI is now supported in Azure Government, including GCC and GCC High.
Government customers can use the Azure Maps visual to bring location-based data to life with interactive map visualizations, making it easier to explore geographic patterns and insights within their government cloud environment.
Learn how to get started with the Azure Maps visual in Power BI.
Plot area background color and transparency (Generally Available)
Match your visuals to your report's design with plot area background color and transparency settings, now available in this release of Power BI Desktop following their announcement in the previous release. Set a background color and adjust its transparency. You can also use conditional formatting and URLs for plot area background images.
Figure: Bar chart with the Plot area background formatting pane open, showing the new Background color and Transparency options.
Learn more about customizing visualization background color and transparency.
Drag and drop navigation ordering in Org Apps
Put your org app's most important content where readers can find it. In edit mode, drag navigation items to reorder them. For example, move a newly added item or link from the bottom of the navigation to the position you want.
Figure: Reorder an org app’s navigation by dragging an item to a new position.
To learn more, refer to the org apps documentation.
Multi-tasking support for Org Apps
You can now switch from editing an org app to another item, such as a Real-Time Dashboard, without being prompted to save or discard your changes. This helps you find and review content to include in the app while you're still building it. An indicator shows when the org app has unsaved changes, as it does for other items.
Figure: A dot beside the org app indicates unsaved changes.
To learn more, refer to the org apps documentation.
Convert existing Org Apps to use audiences
If you created an Org App before audiences were available and don't want to recreate the app entirely, you can now convert it to use audiences. Organize content for different groups within a single app and tailor what each audience sees, rather than creating separate apps for each group.
Figure: Use the Upgrade option to convert an existing org app to use audiences.
To learn more about audiences, refer to the Org Apps (Generally Available) announcement blog post, and the audiences’ conversion documentation.
Apps page updates coming soon; now available in Fabric
The updated Apps page is rolling out progressively and brings Fabric Apps into the browsing experience, along with updated app names, refined sorting, and new pivots. These changes make it easier to browse your apps and find the one you need.
Figure: Org apps, workspace apps, and Fabric apps together on the updated Apps page.
The Apps page is now available in Fabric. To learn more, refer to the updated Apps page documentation.
Modeling
Semantic Views (Preview)
Define your business metrics once, next to your data in OneLake, and use them everywhere. Semantic views let you describe tables, relationships, and business metrics separately from the engines and tools that consume them. For example, define revenue once and reuse the same definition across teams, Power BI reports, and Fabric data agents.
Wherever practical, semantic views are defined in Apache Ossie (incubating) format, a community-led effort to establish a vendor-neutral standard for exchanging semantic metadata across analytics, AI, and BI platforms. Where that is not yet practical, we are working with the community to expand coverage.
With OneLake shortcuts, you can reuse a centrally maintained semantic view across lakehouses without copying it. For example, a regional sales team can use a central revenue definition while keeping its data in its own lakehouse.
In this preview, publishing a semantic view creates a managed, read-only Direct Lake on OneLake semantic model for use in AI and BI experiences. The semantic view remains the source of truth.
To get started, open your lakehouse, select New semantic view, complete the starter YAML or upload your own files, and then select Publish from the semantic view folder.
Use semantic views for definitions shared across tools. Use Power BI semantic models for advanced modeling capabilities.
Figure: Author a semantic view from a Fabric lakehouse.
To learn more, refer to the semantic views documentation.
M parameter support for Direct Lake on OneLake models (Preview)
M parameter support makes it easier to deploy Direct Lake on OneLake semantic models across development, test, and production environments. Use parameter rules in deployment pipelines to point each stage to the appropriate OneLake source without manually updating source expressions in the model after deployment.
You can add parameters through TMDL view, or through Power Query in composite models. Parameterize the workspace and lakehouse IDs separately or use a single parameter for the complete OneLake URI. Then configure stage-specific values using Parameter rules in your deployment pipeline.
This lets you maintain the same semantic model across deployment stages while keeping its OneLake source configuration specific to each environment.
Figure: Define workspace and lakehouse M parameters in TMDL view.Figure: Configure stage-specific M parameter values using Parameter rules in a deployment pipeline.
Learn more in Create deployment rules for Fabric's ALM and Develop Direct Lake semantic models.
Data connectivity
Switch Power Query experiences from Get Data (Preview)
It’s now easier to try the New Power Query Experience (Preview) in Power BI Desktop. You can turn it on or off directly from the Get Data dropdown, without opening Settings.
On the Home ribbon, open the Get Data dropdown and select New Power Query Experience under Get Data (Preview). A check mark shows that it’s enabled. The next time you use Get Data, the new experience opens; no restart required.
Figure: Comparison showing how selecting or clearing New Power Query Experience in Power BI Desktop’s Get Data menu switches between the new and legacy experiences, with no restart required.
Give it a try as you connect to your next data source. You can switch back to the legacy experience by selecting the option again, and Desktop remembers your choice across sessions.
Power BI Mobile
Open Fabric Apps directly in Power BI Mobile (Coming soon) 
Fabric apps are now available directly in the Power BI Mobile app, bringing purpose-built, interactive data experiences to phones and tablets. Users can open a Fabric app without leaving the mobile experience, making it easier to review data, monitor business insights, and act while on the go. 
Fabric apps are integrated into the familiar Power BI Mobile discovery experience. Users can find them from the Apps, Workspaces pages and inside OrgApp navigation, and they can also appear in search, recent items, and favorites.  
After opening a Fabric app, users can use familiar mobile actions, including full-screen viewing, sharing and deep links, in-app search, favorites, and Siri on iOS.  
Figure: Fabric apps can be discovered, opened, and configured for quick access in Power BI Mobile.
For even faster access, users can configure a Fabric app as their launch item. The selected app then opens automatically whenever Power BI Mobile starts, providing one-tap access to a frequently used operational or analytical experience. 
Embedded Analytics 
Embed workspace apps in SharePoint Online (Coming soon)
Power BI Workspace Apps can now be directly embedded into SharePoint Online pages and sites. Previously, you could embed only individual reports and visuals in SharePoint. With this update, you can embed the complete workspace app, including its navigation, sections, and content. Readers get the same experience they would get in Power BI, right on your SharePoint page.
Figure: Embedding a workspace app into a SharePoint Site via a URL.
Two easy ways to add your workspace app

1. Paste the workspace app URL - Open a workspace app in the Power BI Service. On the File menu, select Embed report > SharePoint Online. When embedding a workspace app, you can decide if you want to embed the full app, or just the current report before exporting the URL. Copy the report URL from the dialog box and paste it into the SharePoint content menu. 
2. Choose from the workspace picker - If you don't have the link handy, use the workspace picker in the Power BI web part to browse the workspaces you can access and select the workspace app you want. You don't need to copy or paste a URL.

Whichever way you choose, the embedded workspace app keeps its existing Power BI permissions. Viewers see only content they already have access to, including any audiences you've set up in the app. Your security and governance settings stay in place.
This update supports workspace apps only; support for org apps is planned. Learn how to enable embedding in the Embed a report web part in SharePoint Online documentation.
Third-party custom visuals
Need more visual options for your report? Power BI reports support custom visuals built to fit your exact needs. Browse hundreds of options in AppSource, also available directly from Power BI Desktop, or develop your own and add it to a single report, share it across your organization, or publish it to AppSource for the community. You can even develop a custom visual tailored to your specific requirements with AI coding tools like GitHub Copilot Free. 
The following are some updates from the community-based custom visuals you can use in your reports today. 
Stacked and Layered Waterfall in Zebra BI Charts 
Revenue is 2.1M above plan, and the CFO asks: where did that come from? A waterfall shows how much changed, not which segments drive it, so the review stalls while someone switches pages. 
With Stacked and Layered Waterfall in Zebra BI Charts, one of our most requested features, the total and its drivers sit in one chart. Get the full update. 
Stacked waterfall builds the segments into each column: EMEA +3.2M and Americas +1.4M above the connector, APAC -2.5M below it. Ideal for two or three segments. 
Figure: Stacked waterfall: each monthly variance to plan is broken down by region inside one column.
Layered waterfall gives each segment its own row, with the totals still connected, so the region that broke the quarter can't hide. Ideal for price-volume-mix or cost bridges, where drivers pull in opposite directions. 
Figure: Layered view: each region gets its own row, with the plan and actual totals connected across all rows.
 What you gain: 

Faster reviews: the conversation moves from "where did this come from?" to "what do we do about APAC?" 
Board-ready exports: the breakdown lives in the bars, so it survives PDF and PowerPoint. Nothing to rebuild by hand. 
No extra work: drag a dimension into Groups and switch views with a click. No DAX, no extra measures, and mixed directions split automatically so bar heights stay honest. 

 Try it out in Zebra BI Charts. 
Drill Down Line PRO by ZoomCharts 
Make line charts easier to read and explore with Drill Down Line PRO. Series Labels show each series name beside the chart, with a connector pointing to its line. Users can see which line is which without checking the legend. This helps when comparing sales by region, product results, or actual sales against a budget. 
Figure: The top image showcases the new customizable series labels feature introduced in the Drill Down Line PRO visual. The bottom image demonstrates how to drill down to the next level by selecting a category directly on the chart.
 
Figure: The customization and interactive features of Drill Down Line PRO, including the ability to combine up to 25 data series in a single chart, customize line styles (solid, dashed, dotted, or stepped), highlight key values, and display targets or benchmarks directly on the chart. Interactive navigation allows users to focus on specific chart areas for deeper analysis.
Key features: 

Series Labels: Customize fonts, colors, backgrounds, markers, and connectors to fit your report. Available when the second Y-axis is turned off. 
Click to drill down: Move from a broad view into more detail, such as from regions to individual stores. 
Cross-chart filtering: Select data points to filter other visuals and explore related results. 
Zoom and pan: Focus on the part of the chart you want to explore. 
Up to 25 series: Compare several measures in one chart and style each line separately. 
Flexible line styles: Choose solid, dashed, dotted, or stepped lines. 
Color rules and thresholds: Highlight key values and show targets or benchmarks directly on the chart. 

Get it on AppSource. 
Threadseer: See How Work Really Flows 
Your dashboards show what happened. But can they show how it happened? An order took 12 days to complete. A claim was processed three times. A service request missed its deadline. Traditional dashboards can highlight these outcomes, but understanding the actual sequence of events behind them often requires a different kind of analysis.  
Threadseer brings a comprehensive process mining platform directly into Power BI, turning event-level data into interactive maps of how work really flows through an organization. 
Discover the most common process paths, pinpoint bottlenecks and rework, compare variations, investigate deviations from expected workflows, and drill into individual cases to understand what happened. Whether you're analyzing healthcare claims, manufacturing orders, financial operations, or service requests, Threadseer helps you move from reporting results to investigating the processes behind them. It runs within the Power BI visual, without requiring a separate process mining platform or sending your event data to an external service. Get started with the free Community edition and discover what your existing data can reveal.
Figure: Process Map – Threadseer process mining visualization in Power BI showing a healthcare claims workflow with branching process paths, common variants, rework loops, and activity-level metrics.Figure: Variant Comparison – Threadseer comparing two healthcare claims process variants in Power BI, highlighting differences in workflow steps and median cycle time.
Explore Threadseer on Microsoft Marketplace 
That’s a wrap!
From new ways to build AI-assisted apps and work with Microsoft Copilot to greater flexibility across reporting, modeling, connectivity, and embedded analytics, this month’s updates are designed to help you get more from Power BI.
Try the features that are most relevant to your work, explore the linked documentation to learn more, and let us know what you think. We’ll be back next month with more Power BI updates.
We're sharing this month's updates ahead of the Power BI Desktop release, which will follow the week of November 23, 2026.

Download November Power BI Desktop after November 23, 2026.

new_articles.title: Power BI at Ignite: Building on the momentum
new_articles.summary:
If you haven't already, read Bogdan Crivat's Microsoft Fabric Ignite blog post for a complete look at our Ignite announcements across Microsoft Fabric.
Coming out of FabCon/SQLCon in Barcelona and the Power Platform Community Conference, I'm more excited than ever about what's ahead for Power BI. It's been inspiring to see the community explore new AI-powered experiences and rethink how we interact with data, uncover insights, and make decisions.
At FabCon, I shared that Power BI is entering its next chapter. Your ideas, enthusiasm, and feedback since then have helped shape what we're delivering this week. At Ignite, two key parts of that chapter are ready for you to try: Power BI Desktop for Apps and semantic views, both now in public preview.
Power BI Desktop for Apps: Build apps where you already build reports
In Barcelona, we gave you an early look at a new app-building experience in Power BI Desktop, powered by Fabric apps. This week, it arrives in preview as Power BI Desktop for Apps.
It starts where Power BI always has with a semantic model you already trust. Choose a published semantic model, describe the app you want in natural language, and an agent builds it and iterates with you. Refine the result with direct edits and a design pane, preview it locally, and publish it to Microsoft Fabric when it's ready.
Because these are apps, they can do more than display data. They can accept inputs, preserve shared state, and support operational workflows. That makes room for everything from a focused portal for a team's reports to a planning app where people enter targets, approve them, and comment in context, all built on the definitions your organization already trusts.
Reports aren't going anywhere; they remain the fastest way to explore and share insights. Apps extend what you can build on the same semantic model when people need to act on what they see.
This experience isn't limited to Fabric capacity customers. Apps in Power BI are available to Power BI Pro customers in the coming weeks, with support for Premium Per User coming in the months ahead. Fabric apps, the technology underneath, is also now generally available.
Figure: Creating an app with the new experience in Power BI Desktop.
The apps you build with Power BI Desktop for apps come with a new set of visuals made for Fabric apps. Charts, maps, KPI cards, slicers and data grids share consistent typography, color and spacing, so an app looks cohesive without requiring you to hand-tune every visual. They work in light and dark themes and adapt to your app's own colors.
They also behave the way Power BI users expect. With the Fabric visuals packages you get familiar Power BI capabilities like tooltips, cross-filtering and cross-highlighting, so selecting a point in one visual focuses the rest of the page. They support keyboard navigation and screen readers too.
To learn more about how we're designing visuals for people and agents alike, refer to the blogpost on Data visualization in the agentic era.
Figure: Examples of Fabric visuals capabilities.
Semantic views: an open semantic layer, built on Apache Ossie
The semantic layer is an organization's most strategic asset. With more than 22 million Power BI semantic models in use every day, Power BI is the world's most widely adopted semantic layer, and the business meaning in those models increasingly grounds agents, apps, and Microsoft Copilot.
Today, semantic views enter public preview as the first semantic layer based on Apache Ossie (incubating) open standards, with the unparalleled modeling power of Power BI behind it. You define governed business metrics and semantics directly where your data lives in OneLake, in an open format designed for interoperability. Measures can be written in DAX, so a definition like Total Sales can carry year-over-year and rolling-period logic, not just a simple sum. Define a metric once and reuse it across reports, apps, and AI, within Fabric and, through Apache Ossie, with platforms such as Snowflake and other partners over time.
Semantic models remain the heart of Power BI and Fabric IQ. Semantic views complement them by separating business definitions from compute, so the definitions your teams agree on can move across engines and ecosystems without being rebuilt. We'll keep advancing Apache Ossie with Snowflake and the broader community, including establishing DAX as an Ossie-recognized query language.
Figure: Defining governed business metrics in a semantic view.
What's ahead
If you're ready to take the next step and want to learn how to build apps for your teams and organization, we invite you to join Data Days: AI Work​ to learn from practitioners through real projects, working demos, and follow-along sessions. Whether you want to understand the possibilities, find a pattern to try, or share what you build, explore the sessions and find your next step at aka.ms/DataDays.
Register for our upcoming Fabric and SQL Community Conferences: Atlanta | Sydney—use code MSCUST to save.
Thank you for building with us and for continuing to challenge us to imagine what comes next. I can't wait to see what you create.

General 
Retiring standalone Power BI Copilot experiences in favor of Microsoft Copilot (Preview)
The next chapter for Microsoft Copilot in Power BI and Fabric. We're expanding Microsoft Copilot in Power BI and Fabric to users without a Copilot Premium license. This is the next step toward replacing standalone Power BI Copilot with Microsoft Copilot.
Figure: The Microsoft Chat experience in Power BI; available capabilities depend on your license and entitlements.
The path from standalone Power BI Copilot. We plan to end support for standalone Power BI Copilot on the web, including Home, and in Teams and Power BI mobile by the end of January 2027. These experiences remain available during the transition. Official deprecation, end-of-support, and retirement dates have not been announced; we will share dates and guidance separately. Microsoft Copilot is the planned replacement, with capabilities based on each user's license and entitlements. Report Copilot remains available and supported in the Power BI service, Power BI Desktop, and Power BI mobile. Copilot in web modeling and DAX query view also remains available and supported.
An upgraded experience built around your Fabric data. Power BI and Fabric users without an M365 Copilot Premium license will be able to use Fabric IQ in Microsoft Copilot in the Power BI service even with just a Basic license, subject to their content permissions and licensed access.
Refer to the licensing and eligibility requirements for the applicable access conditions.
With Fabric IQ in the Basic experiences, users can:

Find and reference supported reports by name, link, or attachment.
Ask questions grounded in Power BI semantic models and explore results through follow-up questions.
Return to conversation history across supported Copilot experiences.

Basic licenses include Fabric IQ, but not Work IQ. Premium adds Work IQ for organizational Microsoft 365 emails, meetings, chats, and documents, plus features such as advanced model access.
For more information on the breakdown, refer to the Copilot in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric (Preview) documentation.
Updated Copilot defaults on December 8, 2026. Microsoft Copilot is currently off by default; administrators can enable it in the Fabric admin portal. Admins can manage access with the "Users can access Microsoft Copilot in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric" tenant setting in the Fabric admin portal.
On December 8, 2026, Microsoft Copilot will default to on and standalone Power BI Copilot will default to off. Existing administrator choices will be preserved. This changes tenant-setting defaults only; it is not a deprecation, end-of-support, or retirement date.
Figure: Visual of the Microsoft Copilot tenant setting in the Fabric Admin portal.
Get started
Explore the current preview and administrator requirements in Copilot in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric. For more about how Copilot answers questions using Power BI data, refer to Fabric IQ in Copilot Chat.
Retiring app-scoped Copilot (Preview) in Power BI workspace apps
We're retiring app-scoped Copilot (Preview) in Power BI workspace apps. The experience and the workspace app setup setting used to enable it will be removed in January 2027.
Figure: App-scoped Copilot entry point in a Power BI workspace app navigation menu.
Your app content, audiences, and permissions will remain unchanged. You can continue using Copilot within eligible reports, including reports opened in a workspace app, to ask questions about your data and get summaries.
Power BI Desktop for Apps (Preview)
We're building a new way to turn your Power BI data into interactive Fabric apps.
Power BI Desktop for Apps combines your semantic model with an AI-assisted app-authoring experience. Start with your data, describe the experience you want to create, and work with the built-in agent to build and iterate on your app. You can then preview your app locally and continue refining it yourself.

As you build, a live connection to your semantic model in the Power BI service gives the agent context about your data. You can also edit text directly and use the Design pane to adjust fonts, colors, themes, and other visual properties.
Power BI Desktop for Apps is being prepared for preview and is coming soon. Learn more.
Reporting
Improved performance for the Power BI add-in in PowerPoint
Presentations with multiple Power BI add-ins can now use less memory and load faster. We've improved the Power BI add-in for PowerPoint to reduce its memory footprint and load times, helping PowerPoint handle more Power BI content in a presentation. If you've tried the add-in before, try it again with a presentation that includes several Power BI reports or visuals.
Power BI Integration with OneDrive and SharePoint (Generally Available)
First introduced in 2023, in preview, the Power BI integration with OneDrive and SharePoint has reached general availability.
Many report authors already use OneDrive and SharePoint to store and collaborate on their Power BI files before publishing them. With this release, both the web viewing experience and the open, save, and share capabilities in Power BI Desktop are ready for production use, so your reports can live where the rest of your Microsoft 365 work already does. 
View Power BI files right in OneDrive and SharePoint 
Quickly view Power BI files stored in OneDrive and SharePoint directly in your browser, with no need to install Power BI Desktop or download the file. Just select a .pbix file in your OneDrive or SharePoint library and the report opens in the browser, where you can interact with visuals, explore the data, use bookmarks, switch page views, and apply high-contrast colors. 

Share with confidence: share a link using the familiar Microsoft 365 share dialog, which respects your OneDrive and SharePoint permissions and policies. 
Built-in version history: track changes and restore earlier versions of a report with Microsoft 365 version history. 
Governed by default: sensitivity labels are respected, and admins have visibility through Microsoft 365 audit logs and the Power BI activity log. 

Figure: Power BI reports can be viewed directly in SharePoint or OneDrive.
Open, save, and share from Power BI Desktop 
Power BI Desktop works seamlessly with OneDrive and SharePoint. Open reports straight from your OneDrive or SharePoint sites, save new or existing reports directly to a cloud location, and share a link with colleagues using the Share button at the top right of Power BI Desktop. Storing your files in OneDrive and SharePoint gives you file versioning, easier co-authoring, and a backup that's always in the cloud. 
Figure: Open Power BI files from OneDrive, SharePoint, or your recent files in Power BI Desktop.
 Getting started 

Viewing in the browser is on by default. Admins can manage it under Tenant settings > Integration settings in the admin portal: “Users can view Power BI files saved in OneDrive and SharePoint”.
Open, save, and share in Power BI Desktop are on by default in the November release of Power BI Desktop. Admins can manage it under Tenant settings > Integration settings in the admin portal: “Users can share links to Power BI files stored in OneDrive and SharePoint through Power BI Desktop”.
To view reports in the browser, you need a Power BI Pro, Premium Per User, or E5 license and at least read access to the file. 

Try the Power BI integration with OneDrive and SharePoint and learn more about it in our documentation: View Power BI files in OneDrive and SharePoint and Power BI Desktop OneDrive and SharePoint integration.
Card visual trend charts
Show trends or regional patterns alongside your key metrics in the Card visual. Use a line, bar, or column chart to show changes over time, or a shape map to show regional patterns. To get started, add a field to Trend axis (Preview) in the Build pane. Add measures to compare performance and a legend to identify them. Customize data labels, markers, axes, and other formatting options; tooltips show the data point and axis values.
Figure: The Card visual supports line, column, bar, and shape map charts, with chart and formatting options visible in the Format pane.
Learn more about Card visual trend charts in the Create a card visual in Power BI documentation.
Add to style presets (Generally Available)
Visual style presets let you format a visual once and reuse that formatting for every visual of the same type in your report. Instead of repeating the same changes on each chart, format one visual in the Format visual pane, and then save it as a named style preset or add it to the base visual style.
Figure: Save a visual’s current formatting as a named style preset to reuse across visuals of the same type.
The preset then appears in the Style presets dropdown for every visual of that type, so you can apply the same look with a single selection. You can also make any preset the default for its visual type, and visuals that use the default style update to match. Style presets are saved in your report's theme. To reuse them in other reports, download the theme and import it there.
After saving a style preset, use Reset all style settings to default to remove manual formatting overrides and let the visual use its preset. This new option appears alongside Reset all settings to default and removes only formatting set in the Format visual pane. It preserves conditional formatting, actions, and data-bound elements, such as reference labels.
Figure: Reset formatting overrides to use the visual’s style preset without removing conditional formatting, actions, or data bindings.
Learn more about creating, updating, and sharing presets in the Use visual style presets in Power BI reports documentation.
List slicer with multi-line selection box and dropdown (Generally Available)
The list slicer helps you save space on your report page with a customizable dropdown. Format items with pictures, labels, and conditional formatting, and keep that formatting in dropdown mode. Adjust the dropdown size to fit your report. Selections appear as pills that readers can review and remove. To show more selections before they're grouped into a count pill, turn off Single line under Selection box > Layout.
Figure: WithSingle lineturned off, the selection box fills the visual and shows more selections before they're grouped into a count pill.
Use show selected first to list selected items at the top, making them easier to find in long lists. This option works in the list slicer with or without dropdown mode and is also available in the button slicer.
Learn more about creating and using a list slicer.
Gantt chart updates (Preview)
Make overall progress and individual task progress easier to see in the Gantt visual with column totals and data labels. Configure totals under Columns > Totals and data labels under Rows > Data labels in the Format visual pane. This release also fixes progress bar formatting and keyboard navigation issues and increases default column widths to give task details more room.
Figure: Show overall progress with column totals and display progress percentages beside task bars using data labels in the Gantt visual.
 Learn more about using the Gantt visual in Power BI.
Table and matrix filtering from action buttons within visual title (Preview)
Bring filtering to where report viewers are working with the new Filter action button for table and matrix visuals. Adjust visual-level filters directly on the visual, with the same experience and filter card formatting as the Filters pane. The Filter action button also shows the number of visual-level filters applied to the visual.
To enable it, turn on Action buttons under General in the Format visual pane. Position the button within the title, above, or below, and customize its icons, text, and styling to fit your report. The overlay shows only Filters on this visual; page and report filters are still adjusted in the Filters pane.
Figure: Add a Filter action button so readers can adjust visual-level filters directly from a table or matrix without opening the Filters pane.
For now, this is limited to table and matrix visuals, and we plan to bring it to other visuals in a future release. Action buttons are planned to expand with a Sort button in a future release too.
Learn more about adding action buttons to Power BI visuals.
Slicer mode (date picker, dropdown, list) can be set using custom theme (Generally Available)
Set the slicer mode in a custom report theme to apply a consistent default without configuring each slicer individually. Save the setting in your theme file, then reuse the theme in other reports to keep your preferred slicer experience consistent. If the specified mode isn't compatible with the slicer's column, Power BI automatically switches to a compatible mode.
Learn more about setting visual properties in custom report themes.
Default slicer mode for dates is now “date picker” (Generally Available)
When you add a date column to the Slicer visual, it now starts in Date picker mode, so you can offer flexible date filtering without changing the style first. Readers can choose a specific date or range using the calendar or slider, or use relative selections anchored to today, the first date, or the last date in your data. You can still choose another style under Slicer settings > Options > Style in the Format pane.
Learn more about using the Date picker slicer.
Icons visibility improvements for high contrast mode (Generally Available)
Conditional formatting icons now adjust to display correctly in high contrast mode, making it easier to distinguish status indicators and interpret your data when using high contrast settings.
Figure: Conditional formatting icons now adapt to high contrast mode, including in the icon picker.
Learn more about using high contrast colors in Power BI reports.
Blank reports in the web communicate better next steps (Generally Available)
When you edit a blank report on the web, you now see the same getting-started experience as in Power BI Desktop.
Figure: The blank report canvas on the web now shows the same getting-started guidance as Power BI Desktop, helping authors build visuals from their data.
If a report is intentionally blank with no visuals, viewers see a banner explaining that it's empty, so they don't mistake the blank canvas for content that's still loading.
Figure: A banner lets report viewers know when a report is empty and suggests adding visuals or contacting the report owner.
Learn more about viewing and editing reports in the Power BI service.
Azure Maps support for sovereign clouds (Generally Available)
Azure Maps in Power BI is now supported in Azure Government, including GCC and GCC High.
Government customers can use the Azure Maps visual to bring location-based data to life with interactive map visualizations, making it easier to explore geographic patterns and insights within their government cloud environment.
Learn how to get started with the Azure Maps visual in Power BI.
Plot area background color and transparency (Generally Available)
Match your visuals to your report's design with plot area background color and transparency settings, now available in this release of Power BI Desktop following their announcement in the previous release. Set a background color and adjust its transparency. You can also use conditional formatting and URLs for plot area background images.
Figure: Bar chart with the Plot area background formatting pane open, showing the new Background color and Transparency options.
Learn more about customizing visualization background color and transparency.
Drag and drop navigation ordering in Org Apps
Put your org app's most important content where readers can find it. In edit mode, drag navigation items to reorder them. For example, move a newly added item or link from the bottom of the navigation to the position you want.
Figure: Reorder an org app’s navigation by dragging an item to a new position.
To learn more, refer to the org apps documentation.
Multi-tasking support for Org Apps
You can now switch from editing an org app to another item, such as a Real-Time Dashboard, without being prompted to save or discard your changes. This helps you find and review content to include in the app while you're still building it. An indicator shows when the org app has unsaved changes, as it does for other items.
Figure: A dot beside the org app indicates unsaved changes.
To learn more, refer to the org apps documentation.
Convert existing Org Apps to use audiences
If you created an Org App before audiences were available and don't want to recreate the app entirely, you can now convert it to use audiences. Organize content for different groups within a single app and tailor what each audience sees, rather than creating separate apps for each group.
Figure: Use the Upgrade option to convert an existing org app to use audiences.
To learn more about audiences, refer to the Org Apps (Generally Available) announcement blog post, and the audiences’ conversion documentation.
Apps page updates coming soon; now available in Fabric
The updated Apps page is rolling out progressively and brings Fabric Apps into the browsing experience, along with updated app names, refined sorting, and new pivots. These changes make it easier to browse your apps and find the one you need.
Figure: Org apps, workspace apps, and Fabric apps together on the updated Apps page.
The Apps page is now available in Fabric. To learn more, refer to the updated Apps page documentation.
Modeling
Semantic Views (Preview)
Define your business metrics once, next to your data in OneLake, and use them everywhere. Semantic views let you describe tables, relationships, and business metrics separately from the engines and tools that consume them. For example, define revenue once and reuse the same definition across teams, Power BI reports, and Fabric data agents.
Wherever practical, semantic views are defined in Apache Ossie (incubating) format, a community-led effort to establish a vendor-neutral standard for exchanging semantic metadata across analytics, AI, and BI platforms. Where that is not yet practical, we are working with the community to expand coverage.
With OneLake shortcuts, you can reuse a centrally maintained semantic view across lakehouses without copying it. For example, a regional sales team can use a central revenue definition while keeping its data in its own lakehouse.
In this preview, publishing a semantic view creates a managed, read-only Direct Lake on OneLake semantic model for use in AI and BI experiences. The semantic view remains the source of truth.
To get started, open your lakehouse, select New semantic view, complete the starter YAML or upload your own files, and then select Publish from the semantic view folder.
Use semantic views for definitions shared across tools. Use Power BI semantic models for advanced modeling capabilities.
Figure: Author a semantic view from a Fabric lakehouse.
To learn more, refer to the semantic views documentation.
M parameter support for Direct Lake on OneLake models (Preview)
M parameter support makes it easier to deploy Direct Lake on OneLake semantic models across development, test, and production environments. Use parameter rules in deployment pipelines to point each stage to the appropriate OneLake source without manually updating source expressions in the model after deployment.
You can add parameters through TMDL view, or through Power Query in composite models. Parameterize the workspace and lakehouse IDs separately or use a single parameter for the complete OneLake URI. Then configure stage-specific values using Parameter rules in your deployment pipeline.
This lets you maintain the same semantic model across deployment stages while keeping its OneLake source configuration specific to each environment.
Figure: Define workspace and lakehouse M parameters in TMDL view.Figure: Configure stage-specific M parameter values using Parameter rules in a deployment pipeline.
Learn more in Create deployment rules for Fabric's ALM and Develop Direct Lake semantic models.
Data connectivity
Switch Power Query experiences from Get Data (Preview)
It’s now easier to try the New Power Query Experience (Preview) in Power BI Desktop. You can turn it on or off directly from the Get Data dropdown, without opening Settings.
On the Home ribbon, open the Get Data dropdown and select New Power Query Experience under Get Data (Preview). A check mark shows that it’s enabled. The next time you use Get Data, the new experience opens; no restart required.
Figure: Comparison showing how selecting or clearing New Power Query Experience in Power BI Desktop’s Get Data menu switches between the new and legacy experiences, with no restart required.
Give it a try as you connect to your next data source. You can switch back to the legacy experience by selecting the option again, and Desktop remembers your choice across sessions.
Power BI Mobile
Open Fabric Apps directly in Power BI Mobile (Coming soon) 
Fabric apps are now available directly in the Power BI Mobile app, bringing purpose-built, interactive data experiences to phones and tablets. Users can open a Fabric app without leaving the mobile experience, making it easier to review data, monitor business insights, and act while on the go. 
Fabric apps are integrated into the familiar Power BI Mobile discovery experience. Users can find them from the Apps, Workspaces pages and inside OrgApp navigation, and they can also appear in search, recent items, and favorites.  
After opening a Fabric app, users can use familiar mobile actions, including full-screen viewing, sharing and deep links, in-app search, favorites, and Siri on iOS.  
Figure: Fabric apps can be discovered, opened, and configured for quick access in Power BI Mobile.
For even faster access, users can configure a Fabric app as their launch item. The selected app then opens automatically whenever Power BI Mobile starts, providing one-tap access to a frequently used operational or analytical experience. 
Embedded Analytics 
Embed workspace apps in SharePoint Online (Coming soon)
Power BI Workspace Apps can now be directly embedded into SharePoint Online pages and sites. Previously, you could embed only individual reports and visuals in SharePoint. With this update, you can embed the complete workspace app, including its navigation, sections, and content. Readers get the same experience they would get in Power BI, right on your SharePoint page.
Figure: Embedding a workspace app into a SharePoint Site via a URL.
Two easy ways to add your workspace app

1. Paste the workspace app URL - Open a workspace app in the Power BI Service. On the File menu, select Embed report > SharePoint Online. When embedding a workspace app, you can decide if you want to embed the full app, or just the current report before exporting the URL. Copy the report URL from the dialog box and paste it into the SharePoint content menu. 
2. Choose from the workspace picker - If you don't have the link handy, use the workspace picker in the Power BI web part to browse the workspaces you can access and select the workspace app you want. You don't need to copy or paste a URL.

Whichever way you choose, the embedded workspace app keeps its existing Power BI permissions. Viewers see only content they already have access to, including any audiences you've set up in the app. Your security and governance settings stay in place.
This update supports workspace apps only; support for org apps is planned. Learn how to enable embedding in the Embed a report web part in SharePoint Online documentation.
Third-party custom visuals
Need more visual options for your report? Power BI reports support custom visuals built to fit your exact needs. Browse hundreds of options in AppSource, also available directly from Power BI Desktop, or develop your own and add it to a single report, share it across your organization, or publish it to AppSource for the community. You can even develop a custom visual tailored to your specific requirements with AI coding tools like GitHub Copilot Free. 
The following are some updates from the community-based custom visuals you can use in your reports today. 
Stacked and Layered Waterfall in Zebra BI Charts 
Revenue is 2.1M above plan, and the CFO asks: where did that come from? A waterfall shows how much changed, not which segments drive it, so the review stalls while someone switches pages. 
With Stacked and Layered Waterfall in Zebra BI Charts, one of our most requested features, the total and its drivers sit in one chart. Get the full update. 
Stacked waterfall builds the segments into each column: EMEA +3.2M and Americas +1.4M above the connector, APAC -2.5M below it. Ideal for two or three segments. 
Figure: Stacked waterfall: each monthly variance to plan is broken down by region inside one column.
Layered waterfall gives each segment its own row, with the totals still connected, so the region that broke the quarter can't hide. Ideal for price-volume-mix or cost bridges, where drivers pull in opposite directions. 
Figure: Layered view: each region gets its own row, with the plan and actual totals connected across all rows.
 What you gain: 

Faster reviews: the conversation moves from "where did this come from?" to "what do we do about APAC?" 
Board-ready exports: the breakdown lives in the bars, so it survives PDF and PowerPoint. Nothing to rebuild by hand. 
No extra work: drag a dimension into Groups and switch views with a click. No DAX, no extra measures, and mixed directions split automatically so bar heights stay honest. 

 Try it out in Zebra BI Charts. 
Drill Down Line PRO by ZoomCharts 
Make line charts easier to read and explore with Drill Down Line PRO. Series Labels show each series name beside the chart, with a connector pointing to its line. Users can see which line is which without checking the legend. This helps when comparing sales by region, product results, or actual sales against a budget.

new_articles.title: Power BI at Ignite: Building on the momentum
new_articles.summary:
If you haven't already, read Bogdan Crivat's Microsoft Fabric Ignite blog post for a complete look at our Ignite announcements across Microsoft Fabric.
Coming out of FabCon/SQLCon in Barcelona and the Power Platform Community Conference, I'm more excited than ever about what's ahead for Power BI. It's been inspiring to see the community explore new AI-powered experiences and rethink how we interact with data, uncover insights, and make decisions.
At FabCon, I shared that Power BI is entering its next chapter. Your ideas, enthusiasm, and feedback since then have helped shape what we're delivering this week. At Ignite, two key parts of that chapter are ready for you to try: Power BI Desktop for Apps and semantic views, both now in public preview.
Power BI Desktop for Apps: Build apps where you already build reports
In Barcelona, we gave you an early look at a new app-building experience in Power BI Desktop, powered by Fabric apps. This week, it arrives in preview as Power BI Desktop for Apps.
It starts where Power BI always has with a semantic model you already trust. Choose a published semantic model, describe the app you want in natural language, and an agent builds it and iterates with you. Refine the result with direct edits and a design pane, preview it locally, and publish it to Microsoft Fabric when it's ready.
Because these are apps, they can do more than display data. They can accept inputs, preserve shared state, and support operational workflows. That makes room for everything from a focused portal for a team's reports to a planning app where people enter targets, approve them, and comment in context, all built on the definitions your organization already trusts.
Reports aren't going anywhere; they remain the fastest way to explore and share insights. Apps extend what you can build on the same semantic model when people need to act on what they see.
This experience isn't limited to Fabric capacity customers. Apps in Power BI are available to Power BI Pro customers in the coming weeks, with support for Premium Per User coming in the months ahead. Fabric apps, the technology underneath, is also now generally available.
Figure: Creating an app with the new experience in Power BI Desktop.
The apps you build with Power BI Desktop for apps come with a new set of visuals made for Fabric apps. Charts, maps, KPI cards, slicers and data grids share consistent typography, color and spacing, so an app looks cohesive without requiring you to hand-tune every visual. They work in light and dark themes and adapt to your app's own colors.
They also behave the way Power BI users expect. With the Fabric visuals packages you get familiar Power BI capabilities like tooltips, cross-filtering and cross-highlighting, so selecting a point in one visual focuses the rest of the page. They support keyboard navigation and screen readers too.
To learn more about how we're designing visuals for people and agents alike, refer to the blogpost on Data visualization in the agentic era.
Figure: Examples of Fabric visuals capabilities.
Semantic views: an open semantic layer, built on Apache Ossie
The semantic layer is an organization's most strategic asset. With more than 22 million Power BI semantic models in use every day, Power BI is the world's most widely adopted semantic layer, and the business meaning in those models increasingly grounds agents, apps, and Microsoft Copilot.
Today, semantic views enter public preview as the first semantic layer based on Apache Ossie (incubating) open standards, with the unparalleled modeling power of Power BI behind it. You define governed business metrics and semantics directly where your data lives in OneLake, in an open format designed for interoperability. Measures can be written in DAX, so a definition like Total Sales can carry year-over-year and rolling-period logic, not just a simple sum. Define a metric once and reuse it across reports, apps, and AI, within Fabric and, through Apache Ossie, with platforms such as Snowflake and other partners over time.
Semantic models remain the heart of Power BI and Fabric IQ. Semantic views complement them by separating business definitions from compute, so the definitions your teams agree on can move across engines and ecosystems without being rebuilt. We'll keep advancing Apache Ossie with Snowflake and the broader community, including establishing DAX as an Ossie-recognized query language.
Figure: Defining governed business metrics in a semantic view.
What's ahead
If you're ready to take the next step and want to learn how to build apps for your teams and organization, we invite you to join Data Days: AI Work​ to learn from practitioners through real projects, working demos, and follow-along sessions. Whether you want to understand the possibilities, find a pattern to try, or share what you build, explore the sessions and find your next step at aka.ms/DataDays.
Register for our upcoming Fabric and SQL Community Conferences: Atlanta | Sydney—use code MSCUST to save.
Thank you for building with us and for continuing to challenge us to imagine what comes next. I can't wait to see what you create.
